overview.text: Coral reefs are complex marine ecosystems built chiefly by reef-building stony corals. A coral is often a colony of tiny animals called polyps; each secretes a hard calcium-carbonate skeleton, and generations of growth add to the reef’s foundation. Many reef-building corals also partner with microscopic algae that provide food through photosynthesis. The reef’s three-dimensional structure offers habitat, food, and shelter for a wide range of marine life, while reefs also benefit people by supporting food resources and helping protect shorelines. Reef forms include fringing reefs along coasts, barrier reefs farther offshore, and atolls—rings of coral surrounding a lagoon.

key_facts.text: Corals are animals; most corals form colonies of polyps, though some are solitary.
Stony corals secrete calcium-carbonate skeletons that build the reef foundation; dead skeletons continue to add structure and habitat.
Many reef-building corals exchange resources with photosynthetic algae living in their tissues; the algae supply food that helps corals grow.
An atoll is a ring-shaped coral reef surrounding a lagoon; barrier reefs also lie offshore, separated from land by a lagoon.
Bleaching occurs when stressed corals expel symbiotic algae and turn white; a bleached coral is not necessarily dead, though it is under stress.
